figure_1_2.title: Self-driven/distrusting young men are most likely to have felt pressure to conform.

figure_1_3.title: Most young men believe women have unrealistic expectations.

figure_1_5.title: Being the sole provider is an important element of success for most young men.

figure_1_6.title: Young men are less likely than young women and older men to agree with equal opportunity and equal pay.

figure_1_7.title: Ninety percent of relational/distrusting young men agree with equal opportunity and equal pay. Fewer self-driven/trusting young men agree.

figure_2_1.title: Many young men believe college is a questionable investment.

figure2_2.title: Many young men believe colleges do not align with workplace needs.

figure_2_3.title: Young men believe colleges are designed to benefit women.

figure_2_4.title: Most self-driven/distrusting young men believe men should have physically demanding jobs.

figure_2_5.title: Most self-driven/distrusting young men, even those who are Democrats, agree that people without liberal political views are not welcome at colleges.

figure_2_6.title: Young men view trade schools and bachelor’s degrees as holding similar value.

figure_2_7.title: Relational/distrusting young men are most likely to see the value of obtaining a bachelor’s degree or higher in today’s job market.

figure_2_9.title: More young men than young women did not seriously consider pursuing a degree after high school.

figure_2_11.title: Affordability, uncertainty about what to study, and a preference for full-time work are the main reasons young men say they do not pursue a degree after high school.

figure_2_12.title: More young Black than Latino or white young men did not pursue a degree after high school because of a major life event. Fewer young Black men than their Latino or white peers cite costs.

figure_2_13.title: Black and Latino young men are more likely than their white peers to report financial impacts from not obtaining a degree.

figure_2_14.title: Self-driven/distrusting young men without degrees are most likely to experience financial and social impacts from the lack of a credential.

figure_2_15.title: Self-driven/distrusting young men are most likely to regret pursuing their degree

figure_2_16.title: Young Latino men are most likely to report they would like to earn a degree but face various barriers.

figure_2_17.title: Many young men without degrees would like to earn one, but they see barriers.

figure_2_18.title: More young men than women pursued a college degree to build professional networks.

figure_2_19.title: Young men who have a degree are more likely than those without a degree to believe hard work will lead to success.

figure_2_20b.title: Young men with degrees report their college education was useful in helping them grow personally, professionally, and socially.

figure_2_22.title: Relational/distrusting young men are most likely to say reducing tuition would help a lot to make college a safer investment.

figure_2_23.title: Young men trust community-based organizations more than the government to help make college a better investment.

figure_2_24.title: Self-driven/distrusting young men believe employers and industry coalitions are a plausible group to make college a better investment.

figure_3_1.title: Young men and young women report feeling disconnected and irrelevant at similar rates.

figure_3_2.title: Relational/distrusting and self-driven/distrusting young men are especially likely to have felt lonely or irrelevant.

figure_3_3.title: Disconnection and irrelevance is lower among relational/distrusting young men who have a degree than those without. This is not true for the self-driven/distrusting peers.

figure_3_5b.title: Most relational and self-driven/distrusting young men want more people to connect with and most wish they had deeper connections.
